en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Vessantara, Concerning the Question of Inference.
8. The Question on the Realization of the Dhamma “Venerable Nāgasena, for all those who practice rightly, does the realization of the Dhamma occur for them all, or does it not occur for some?
“For some, Great King, it occurs; for others, it does not,” [he replied].
“Venerable sir, for whom does it exist, and for whom does it not exist?
“For one who has been reborn as an animal, great king—even if he has practiced rightly—there is no realization of the Dhamma;
nor for one reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts… nor for one of wrong view… nor for a hypocrite… nor for a matricide… nor for a patricide… nor for a murderer of an arahant.”

… for one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha … for one who sheds blood [of a Buddha] … for one living in communion by theft … for one who has gone over to another sect … for one who has violated a bhikkhunī … for one who,
having committed any one of the thirteen heavy offenses, has not made amends … for a paṇḍaka … for one with both sexual organs;
even for these who have practiced well, there is no realization of the Dhamma … and also for one who—
"A child-eater is one who is less than seven years old; even though he may practice rightly, there is no realization of the Dhamma for him.
It is for these sixteen types of persons, O Great King, that there is no realization of the Dhamma, even though they practice rightly.
"Venerable Nāgasena, as for those fifteen types of persons who are indeed obstructed, let there be realization of the Dhamma for them."
Whether it be so or not, for what reason does the realization of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*) not occur even for a well-practicing human child less than seven years of age?
In this regard, the question arises: "Is it not the case that a child possesses neither lust (*rāga*), nor hatred (*dosa*), nor delusion (*moha*)?"
“There is no conceit, no wrong view, no aversion, and no sensual thought;
he is unmixed with defilements. Such a youth, being disciplined and mature, is indeed worthy to penetrate the Four Truths through a single penetration.
“Great King, that is precisely the reason why I say: ‘For one who is less than seven years old, even if they have practiced rightly, there is no realization of the Dhamma.’”
If, Great King, one who is less than seven years old could be stained by what is provocative of passion, corrupted by what is provocative of hatred, deluded by what is provocative of delusion,
intoxicated by what is provocative of intoxication, discern right view, discern both pleasure and displeasure, and reflect upon the wholesome and the unwholesome,
then there might be for him the realization of the Dhamma. However, Great King, for one who is less than seven years old—
The mind is weak, feeble, limited, slight, trifling, dull, and unmanifest;
whereas the unconditioned element of Nibbāna is heavy, weighty, vast, and great.

One who is less than seven years old, O Great King, by means of that weak, limited, dull, and unmanifest mind, is not able to penetrate the unconditioned element of Nibbāna, which is heavy, weighty, vast, and great.
“Great king, just as Sineru, the king of mountains, is heavy, burdensome, vast, and great— would a man,
by means of his own ordinary strength, power, and energy, be able to lift up Sineru, the king of mountains? “Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“For what reason, Great King?
“Because of the weakness of the person, venerable sir, and because of the greatness of Sineru, the king of mountains.

“In the same way, Great King, the mind of one less than seven years old is weak, feeble, limited, small, trifling, dull, and undeveloped; whereas the unconditioned element of Nibbāna is heavy, weighty, vast, and great.”
One who is less than seven years old, with that weak, limited, dull, and unmanifest mind,
is unable to penetrate the profound, weighty, vast, great, and unconditioned element of Nibbāna; for that reason,
even one who has practiced well for less than seven years does not achieve the realization of the Dhamma.
Or again, great king, suppose this great earth were long, extended, broad, wide, vast, expansive, and immense;
would it be possible, great king, to moisten that great earth with a tiny drop of water and turn it into a muddy quagmire?”
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“For what reason, great king?
“Because, venerable sir, the drop of water is small and the great earth is vast.”
“In the same way, Great King, the mind of one less than seven years old is weak,
feeble, limited, small, trifling, dull, and unmanifest; whereas the unconditioned element of Nibbāna is long,
extended, broad, wide, vast, expansive, abundant, and great.”
One who is less than seven years old, with that weak, limited, dull, and unmanifest mind,
is unable to penetrate the great, unconditioned element of Nibbāna; for that reason, even one who has practiced well,
if they are less than seven years old, does not achieve the realization of the Dhamma.
"Or again, great king, suppose there were a weak, feeble, small, slight, and dim fire.
Would it be possible, great king, by means of such a dim fire to dispel the darkness in the world with its devas and show forth light?
"Certainly not, venerable sir."
“For what reason, Great King?
“Because of the dullness of the fire, venerable sir, and because of the vastness of the world.
“In the same way, Great King, the mind of one less than seven years old is weak, feeble, limited, small, trifling, dull, and unmanifest; it is shrouded by the great darkness of ignorance.”
Therefore, it is difficult to manifest the light of knowledge; for that reason, even one who has practiced well for less than seven years does not achieve the realization of the Dhamma.

Or again, Great King, it is as if a sickly, emaciated, and minute *sālakakimi* insect were to encounter an elephant-king at its own place—three-fold in height, nine-fold in length, ten-fold in girth, and eighteen cubits in stature.
“Having seen it, would he drag it toward himself to swallow it? Would that *sālakakimi* worm, O Great King, be able to swallow that noble elephant?
“No, venerable sir.
“For what reason, Great King?”
“Because of the smallness of the *sālakakimi*, venerable sir, and the greatness of the noble elephant.
“In the same way, great king, the mind of one less than seven years old is weak, feeble, limited, slight, meager, dull, and unmanifest; whereas the great, unconditioned element of Nibbāna is vast.
With that weak, limited, dull, and unmanifest mind, he is not able [to grasp] the great, unconditioned [Nibbāna].”
“Because one must penetrate the element of Nibbāna, for that reason there is no realization of the Dhamma for one who is less than seven years old, even if they have practiced well.
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; I accept it as you have said.”
The eighth question: On the Realization of the Dhamma.
